posts.title: How much does it cost to build a web app in the UK?
posts.excerpt: An honest breakdown of what drives the cost of a web app, how freelancers, agencies and off-the-shelf tools compare, and how to keep your first version affordable.
posts.seoDescription: What does a web app cost to build in the UK? An honest guide to what drives the price, freelancer vs agency, and how to keep your first version affordable.
posts.body:
"How much will it cost?" is the first question almost everyone asks, and the honest answer is: it depends on what you're building. That's not a dodge. Two apps that sound similar can differ in price by a factor of five. This post explains what actually drives the cost, so you can work out a realistic budget before you talk to anyone.

## What you're actually paying for

A web app isn't one thing. The price is the sum of a few building blocks, and each one adds time.

**1. The number of screens and features.** Every screen needs designing, building and testing. A tool with a login, a dashboard and one main feature is a very different job from one with ten user roles and fifty screens.

**2. User accounts and permissions.** Letting people sign up and log in securely is standard now, but it still takes work: password resets, email verification, and different permissions for staff, customers and admins.

**3. Payments.** Taking a one-off payment is fairly simple. Subscriptions, free trials, refunds, invoices and VAT handling add up quickly.

**4. Integrations.** Connecting to other systems (your accounting software, a booking tool, a CRM, an API from your industry) is often where the surprises are. A well-documented integration might take a day. A messy one can take weeks.

**5. Design.** Using a clean, proven layout is quicker than a fully custom design with animations and illustrations. Both are valid; they just cost differently.

**6. What happens after launch.** Hosting, security updates, backups and bug fixes are ongoing costs. Any quote that doesn't mention them is only telling you half the story.

## Rough price ranges

> **TODO: add your own figures here.** Give honest ranges for what you'd charge, and if you include market comparisons, only use numbers you're confident in.

- A simple internal tool or prototype: TODO
- A web app MVP with accounts and payments: TODO (my Web App MVP package starts at TODO)
- A larger platform with several user types and integrations: TODO
- Ongoing hosting, updates and support: TODO per month

## Freelancer, agency or off-the-shelf?

**Off-the-shelf software** is cheapest if it genuinely fits. You pay a monthly fee and get started today. The catch is that you shape your business around the tool, not the other way round. I've written a separate post on [when off-the-shelf is the better choice](/blog/do-you-really-need-a-custom-app).

**An agency** gives you a team: project managers, designers and several developers. That's valuable for large projects, but you're paying for the overhead, and your project may be handed between people.

**A freelancer** usually costs less for the same work, and you deal with the person actually building it. The trade-off is capacity: one person can only take on so much, so it suits focused projects better than huge ones.

## How to keep your first version affordable

The best way to control cost is to build less, at least at first.

1. **Write down the one job the app must do.** If it only did that, would people still use it? That's your MVP.
2. **Move everything else to a "later" list.** Reports, admin dashboards, integrations and nice-to-haves can follow once real users tell you what they need.
3. **Use proven building blocks.** Payments, login and email have solid, existing services. Building those from scratch is rarely worth it.
4. **Agree a fixed scope and price up front.** You should know what you're getting, and what it costs, before work starts.

## The bottom line

A focused first version, built well and launched quickly, nearly always beats a big build that takes a year. If you have an idea and want a realistic number for it, [see my packages](/services) or [get in touch](/contact) and I'll give you an honest estimate.

posts.title: Do you really need a custom app? When off-the-shelf software is the better choice
posts.excerpt: Custom software isn't always the answer. Here's how to tell when an existing tool will do the job better and cheaper, and when building your own really pays off.
posts.seoDescription: Custom app or off-the-shelf software? An honest guide for small businesses on when existing tools are the better choice, and when custom development pays off.
posts.body:
I build custom software for a living, so it might seem odd to write a post telling you not to buy it. But I'd rather you spend your money well. A lot of the time, an existing tool will do the job better, sooner and for a fraction of the price.

Here's how I think about it when someone asks me whether they need a custom app.

## When off-the-shelf is the better choice

**Your problem is common.** If thousands of other businesses have the same need, someone has probably built a good tool for it. Selling products online, taking bookings, sending invoices and running a mailing list are all solved problems. Shopify, Squarespace, Calendly-style booking tools, Xero and Mailchimp exist for a reason.

**You need it working this week.** Existing software is ready now. Even a small custom build takes weeks.

**Your budget is tight.** A monthly subscription is far easier on cash flow than a development project, especially while you're still proving the idea.

**You're not sure how it should work yet.** If you don't know the process, a spreadsheet or a no-code tool lets you experiment cheaply. You'll learn what you actually need, and that makes any custom build later much better.

## When custom software pays off

**You're bending your business around the tool.** If your team spends hours on workarounds, copying data between systems or fighting software that "nearly" fits, that time has a real cost.

**The software *is* the product.** If you're selling the app itself (a SaaS, a platform, a client portal), you need to own it and control how it works.

**You're paying for lots of features you never use.** Sometimes a focused tool that does one thing well is cheaper over a few years than an expensive platform where you use two features.

**You need things to talk to each other.** If the real problem is connecting several systems, a small custom app in the middle can save a surprising amount of time.

## A quick checklist

Ask yourself:

- Have I tried at least two existing tools properly?
- Can I describe, in one sentence, what they can't do?
- Roughly how many hours a month do the workarounds cost us?
- Will this still matter in two years?
- Am I happy to pay for hosting and updates once it's built?

If you answered "yes" to the first and can answer the rest clearly, custom software might well be worth it. If not, start with an existing tool. You can always build later, and you'll know far more about what you need.

## When you don't need me

If an existing tool does 90% of what you need, use it. If you're still working out how your business process runs, start with a spreadsheet. And if you only need a simple brochure site, a good website builder may be all you need.

If you've weighed it up and still think custom is right, or you'd just like a second opinion, [get in touch](/contact). I'll tell you honestly whether I think you need me.
